pages.title: The whole field was building models the wrong size
pages.subtitle: What this paper claims, and why it shook the LLM scaling consensus

blocks.html: By 2022, the recipe for a better language model seemed obvious: make it bigger. GPT-3 had 175B parameters, Gopher 280B, Megatron-Turing NLG 530B. Everyone raced to add parameters. This paper asks a deceptively simple question: given a fixed compute budget, how should you split it between model size and the amount of training data? The shocking answer is that the giant models of the era were far too big and trained on far too little data.

The headline finding: for compute-optimal training, model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally. Double your compute, and you should make the model ~1.4x bigger and train on ~1.4x more data — not pour it all into parameters. As a rule of thumb that became famous: you want roughly 20 tokens of training data per parameter.
We find that current large language models are significantly undertrained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of training data constant.

To prove it, they trained Chinchilla: a 70B-parameter model — four times smaller than Gopher — but on 4x more data (1.4 trillion tokens), using the exact same compute budget as Gopher. Chinchilla then beats Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) on a wide range of evaluations.
Chinchilla uniformly and significantly outperforms Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) on a large range of downstream evaluation tasks.

The bonus: a smaller model is cheaper to use. Every query to Chinchilla costs ~4x less compute than Gopher, and fine-tuning and inference get easier too. So the 'optimal' model is not just better — it is also lighter to deploy. This single insight redirected how the entire field allocates compute.

pages.title: The compute budget is a fixed pie — how do you slice it?
pages.subtitle: Why model size and data are in tension under a fixed FLOP budget

blocks.html: Training a large model has one dominant cost: compute, measured in FLOPs (floating-point operations). You rarely get unlimited compute — you get a budget, set by how many GPUs/TPUs you have and for how long. Every design choice has to fit inside that budget. The two biggest knobs are the number of parameters $N$ and the number of training tokens $D$.
Here is the crucial fact that makes this a real trade-off: for a transformer, the training compute is approximately the product of the two.

Reading it term by term: $C$ is the total training compute in FLOPs (a scalar). $N$ is the number of model parameters. $D$ is the number of training tokens the model sees. The constant 6 comes from counting operations in a transformer — roughly 2 FLOPs per parameter for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass, per token. So if you want to double the model size $N$ but keep compute $C$ fixed, you must halve the data $D$. They fight over the same pie.

Concrete example. Gopher had $N = 280\text{B}$ parameters and was trained on $D = 300\text{B}$ tokens. Its budget was about $C \approx 6 \times (2.8\times10^{11}) \times (3\times10^{11}) \approx 5\times10^{23}$ FLOPs. The paper's claim is that with that same $5\times10^{23}$ FLOPs, a better choice is $N \approx 70\text{B}$ and $D \approx 1.4\text{T}$ — a quarter of the parameters, but 4.7x the data. Same pie, sliced very differently.

blocks.text: Why the previous answer was wrong

blocks.html: Kaplan et al. (2020) — the original 'scaling laws' paper from OpenAI — had studied this and concluded you should put most new compute into parameters and increase data only mildly. That recommendation is what produced the era of giant, data-starved models. Chinchilla's authors redo the experiment more carefully and find the opposite: parameters and data should scale in equal proportion. Pinning down why Kaplan's estimate was off is much of the paper's technical content.

Formally, the goal is to find the functions $N_{opt}(C)$ and $D_{opt}(C)$ that minimize the final loss $L$ subject to the budget constraint $C \approx 6ND$. The next pages walk through the three independent methods they use to estimate them — and reassuringly, all three agree.

pages.title: Three roads to the same answer
pages.subtitle: Approach 1 (IsoFLOP curves) and the equal-scaling result

blocks.html: A claim this consequential needs to be robust, not an artifact of one fitting choice. So the authors estimate the optimal $N(C)$ and $D(C)$ three different ways, with different assumptions, and check that they converge. If three independent methods agree, you trust the answer. Here is the cleanest one to picture: Approach 2, IsoFLOP profiles.

Pick a fixed compute budget — say $6\times10^{18}$ FLOPs. Now train many models at exactly that budget, but trade off size vs. data: a tiny model on lots of tokens, a small model on fewer, a medium model on fewer still, and so on. Because $C$ is fixed, every model along this 'IsoFLOP' (equal-FLOP) curve uses the same compute. Plot each model's final loss against its parameter count, and you get a U-shaped curve: too-small models underfit, too-big models run out of data, and the bottom of the U is the optimal size for that budget.

Concrete example. At $6\times10^{18}$ FLOPs the valley sits near a few hundred million parameters; train a model 4x bigger and loss rises because it saw too little data; train one 4x smaller and loss rises because it lacked capacity. Repeat the whole sweep at $10^{19}$, $10^{20}$, $10^{21}$ FLOPs — you get a nest of U-curves (the paper's Figure 3), and the valley bottoms march steadily to the right (bigger $N$) and down (lower loss) as the budget grows.
Connect the valley bottoms across budgets and you have measured $N_{opt}(C)$ directly. Fit a power law to those optimal points.

Reading it: $N_{opt}$ is the optimal parameter count and $D_{opt}$ the optimal token count, each as a power of the compute budget $C$. The exponents $a$ and $b$ say how fast each should grow. If $a = b = 0.5$, then size and data grow at the same rate — square-root of compute each — which is exactly the 'scale them equally' headline.

All three land near $a \approx b \approx 0.5$. By contrast, Kaplan et al. had reported $a \approx 0.73$, $b \approx 0.27$ — heavily favoring parameters. The gap between $0.5$ and $0.73$ is the entire reason the era's models were oversized. The authors trace Kaplan's discrepancy partly to using a fixed learning-rate schedule rather than one that decays to match each run's token count.

pages.title: A formula for loss as a function of size and data
pages.subtitle: Approach 3: the parametric loss and where the optimum comes from

blocks.html: The IsoFLOP method measures the optimum but does not explain it. Approach 3 fits an actual equation for the loss as a function of $N$ and $D$. Once you have that equation, you can derive the optimal allocation analytically — and you can extrapolate to budgets far larger than anything you trained. This is the most powerful and most reusable of the three methods.
They propose this functional form for the final pre-training loss (a classical decomposition going back to risk-decomposition ideas):

Reading every term. $\hat{L}(N,D)$ is the predicted loss (nats per token) for a model of $N$ parameters trained on $D$ tokens. $E$ is the irreducible loss — the entropy of natural text itself, the floor you could never beat even with infinite model and infinite data. $\frac{A}{N^{\alpha}}$ is the capacity error: how much a finite-size model falls short of a perfect transformer; it shrinks as $N$ grows. $\frac{B}{D^{\beta}}$ is the optimization/data error: how much a model trained on only $D$ tokens (for a single epoch, not to convergence) falls short; it shrinks as you feed more data. $A$, $B$, $\alpha$, $\beta$ are positive constants fit to the data.

The fitted values from their ~400 training runs: $E \approx 1.69$, $A \approx 406.4$, $B \approx 410.7$, $\alpha \approx 0.34$, $\beta \approx 0.28$. The near-equality of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is the secret: because the two error terms decay at nearly the same rate, the cheapest way to drive the loss down is to shrink both terms together — i.e., grow $N$ and $D$ in lockstep.
Now minimize $\hat{L}(N,D)$ subject to $C = 6ND$. This is a textbook Lagrange-multiplier problem. The solution gives the optimal split as power laws in compute:

blocks.tex: N_{opt}(C) = G\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{a}, \qquad D_{opt}(C) = G^{-1}\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{b}, \qquad a = \frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}, \;\; b = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}

blocks.html: Reading it: $N_{opt}$ and $D_{opt}$ are the compute-optimal parameter and token counts; $G$ is a constant set by $A,B,\alpha,\beta$. The key result is in the exponents: $a = \beta/(\alpha+\beta)$ and $b = \alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$, which always sum to 1. Plugging in $\alpha \approx 0.34$, $\beta \approx 0.28$ gives $a \approx 0.46$ and $b \approx 0.54$ — once again, near $0.5$ each. The mathematics forces equal scaling whenever $\alpha \approx \beta$.

Why this matters practically. Because $a+b = 1$, the equation also lets you read off the token-to-parameter ratio at the optimum: it stays roughly constant at ~20 tokens per parameter across budgets. That is the number practitioners now quote. Want a compute-optimal 10B model? Train it on ~200B tokens. A 70B model? ~1.4T tokens — which is exactly Chinchilla.

pages.title: Building the model the theory ordered
pages.subtitle: Chinchilla vs Gopher: same compute, very different shape

blocks.html: A scaling law is a prediction; the only way to test it is to build the predicted model and see if it wins. The authors take Gopher's exact compute budget ($\approx 5.76\times10^{23}$ FLOPs) and ask their fitted laws: what is the optimal $(N, D)$ for that budget? The answer comes back ~70B parameters and ~1.4T tokens. So they train precisely that model and name it Chinchilla.

Same compute, but the shape is inverted: Chinchilla is 4x smaller and trained on ~4.7x more data. Crucially, the comparison is fair — same budget, same training data distribution (MassiveText), same tokenizer (mostly), and a learning-rate schedule properly decayed to match the longer token horizon. Everything is held constant except the size/data split the paper is testing.

The result. Chinchilla beats Gopher essentially everywhere. The flagship number is MMLU (a 57-subject knowledge and reasoning benchmark): Chinchilla scores 67.6%, beating Gopher's 60.0% by 7.6 points and surpassing the average human expert. On language-modeling and reading-comprehension benchmarks the win is broad and consistent, not cherry-picked.
Chinchilla outperforms Gopher and the other large models on the vast majority of these language modelling tasks.

And it is cheaper at every stage after training. With a quarter of the parameters, inference uses ~4x less compute and memory, fine-tuning is lighter, and the model fits more easily on serving hardware. The compute-optimal model is the gift that keeps giving: you pay the same to train it and then save forever on every query.

Why it works. Gopher's 280B parameters were a vast, under-exploited capacity — like a library with millions of shelves but only enough books to fill a quarter of them. The model had room to learn far more than its 300B tokens could teach it. Redirecting that wasted capacity-budget into 4x more data filled the shelves, and the data-starved error term $B/D^{\beta}$ dropped sharply while the capacity term barely rose.

pages.title: The rule that re-sized an entire field
pages.subtitle: What Chinchilla changed, and the asterisks worth knowing

blocks.html: Chinchilla did not introduce a new architecture or a clever trick. Its contribution is a corrected scaling law and a single memorable rule — ~20 tokens per parameter — that immediately changed how labs spend compute. After this paper, the race to ever-larger parameter counts cooled, and the focus shifted to gathering and curating far more training data for more modestly sized models.

Direct lineage. Meta's LLaMA (2023) took the lesson and ran past it: a 7B model trained on 1T tokens, a 13B on 1T — deliberately over-trained relative to Chinchilla-optimal, because at inference time a smaller-but-overtrained model is cheaper to serve. This 'inference-aware' twist is the natural sequel: Chinchilla optimizes training compute, but if you will serve billions of queries, paying extra training to shrink the model further is worth it.

The key reframe. Chinchilla shifted the bottleneck of progress from parameters to data. If optimal training needs ~20x more tokens than people were using, then the supply of high-quality text becomes the binding constraint — a realization that drove the field's later obsession with data quality, deduplication, and eventually the 'are we running out of tokens?' debate.

items: The laws are fit over budgets up to ~1e24 FLOPs; extrapolating many orders of magnitude beyond that is an assumption, not a guarantee.
The ~20:1 ratio is the optimum for minimizing training loss for a single epoch — it ignores inference cost, which is why LLaMA-style overtraining can be the better real-world choice.
All runs use a single pass over data (no repeated epochs); whether the laws hold when you re-use tokens was an open question the paper does not settle.
Bigger high-quality datasets raise toxicity, bias, and data-contamination concerns that scaling laws alone do not address.

blocks.html: The lasting lesson. Before Chinchilla, 'state of the art' meant 'most parameters.' After it, the question became 'are you compute-optimal?' — and the answer for nearly every model of the GPT-3 era was a resounding no. A 70B model beating a 530B one on equal compute is the kind of result that does not just improve the leaderboard; it rewrites the playbook.
